'''''Nageia nagi''''', or the '''Asian bayberry''', is a species of [[conifer]] in the family [[Podocarpaceae]]. ''Nageia nagi'' is native to China, Japan, and Taiwan.<ref name="Nag1"/>

==Description==
[[File:Nageia pollen cones.jpg|thumb|left|''Nageia nagi'' pollen cones]]
[[File:Podocarpus nagi nagi01.jpg|thumb|left|''Nageia nagi'' [[conifer cone|seed cones]]]]
''Nageia nagi'' is a hardy tree species that can withstand a range of weather conditions, but it prefers moist sites that are well drained and with full sunlight to light shade. Being from the family Podocarpaceae, it is a [[dioecious]] tree, that is, the male and female parts of the trees are on separate plants.<ref name="Nag1"/> The pollen cones are similar to [[catkin]]s and the female cones, which mature in one year, are reduced fleshy bracts that contain a single inverted ovule. It requires wind for pollination; it cannot self-pollinate.<ref>{{cite web|title=Podocarpaceae|url=http://www.conifers.org/po/Podocarpaceae.php |publisher=The gymnosperm database|access-date=23 March 2012}}</ref>

The trees range from fifteen to twenty meters in height and are relatively slow growing.<ref name=Nag2>{{cite web |title=Nageia nagi/Asian Bayberry |url=http://www.onlineplantguide.com/PlantDetails.aspx?Plant_id=1728 |publisher=OnlinePlantGuide |access-date=23 March 2012}}</ref> The leaves are lanceolate in shape, and are arranged sub opposite on the branches. Leaves range from two to eight inches long and 0.75 to 2.5 inches wide and lack a mid-vein.  The new leaves are a light green and as they age they become dark green and glossy. The branches also start out as green but as they age they become reddish brown and peel in small layers.<ref name= "Nag1">{{cite web|title=Nageia nagi - Asian Bayberry|url=http://www.plantoftheweek.org/week376.shtml|access-date=23 March 2012}}</ref>

''Nageia nagi'' can be propagated by cuttings or by seed. It is best to plant the seed in a warm greenhouse and sandy soil. For their permanent position, they should be planted in late spring or early summer after the last frost.<ref name="Nag4"/>

The species is threatened by [[habitat loss]].

==Uses==
Houses, bridges, utensils, handiwork and furniture are constructed from the wood. The seeds yield an oil that is edible and valued in industry.<ref name=Nag3>{{cite web|title=Flora of China|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=210001313 |publisher=FOC Vol. 4 Page 80|access-date=23 March 2012}}</ref> Young leaves are sometimes cooked and eaten.<ref name= "Nag4">{{cite web |title=Nageia nagi - (Thunb.)Kuntze |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Nageia+nagi|publisher=Plants For A Future, 1996-2010 |access-date=23 March 2012}}</ref> Its bark exhibits strong antibacterial effect.<ref>Bin Shan, Yi-Zhong Cai, John D. Brooks, Harold Corke (2007). "The in vitro antibacterial activity of dietary spice and medicinal herb extracts". ''International Journal of Food Microbiology'' 117 112–119.</ref> Stems are used in floral arrangements that last in water for up to a year.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nagi Greenery|url=https://flowermoxie.com/products/nagi-greenery|access-date=2021-11-14|website=Flower Moxie|language=en}}</ref>
